response.text:
Mean pooling raw learned item embeddings is permutation invariant: [A,A,B,C] and [C,A,B,A] give identical representations, losing recency, spacing and transitions. Repetition still affects relative composition; [A,A,B,C] generally differs from [A,B,C,D]. However, [A,B] and [A,A,B,B] have identical means, so absolute multiplicity and valid-window length are ambiguous. This matches the distinction between distribution-sensitive mean aggregation and multiset-sensitive sum aggregation in [Xu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826). If “normalized” additionally means L2 normalization, vector magnitude is also discarded. Everything before the four-item window is unavailable to this pooled feature.

Algebraically, sum pooling plus valid count, (s,n), retains the mean because μ=s/n while explicitly exposing window size. Mean plus count is equivalently informative. With exactly four valid items, sum is merely four times the mean; it adds no information. Neither operation preserves order or guarantees recovery of individual item counts from arbitrary learned embeddings. Normalizing the sum immediately removes its scale advantage. Window count saturates at four; expose full-history length separately if needed, and mask padding correctly.

Minimal internal alternatives, inferred from these properties: concatenate masked sum and count with NextItNet’s final nonpadding hidden state; or use learned relative-position weights, position-specific projections, or a small MLP over four ordered embeddings. Simply adding positional embeddings before an ordinary sum still loses item–position association. Softmax attention can encode recency but does not guarantee multiplicity sensitivity. [NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) already models ordered dependencies through dilated convolutions; retain that backbone and train these features jointly within the same model. They require no pretrained models or independent predictors. Their validation benefit remains an empirical question.
